- Nikolsky sign is negative; a positive sign might suggest SSSS

mss-e63ac754a794831d670e.text: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is characterized by epidermolysis of the stratum {{c1::granulosum}}
mss-e63ac754a794831d670e.extra:
- Blistering only occurs in the superficial epidermis (cleavage of desmoglein in desmosomes)

- Important distinguishing feature from toxic epidermal necrolysis, which separates at the dermal-epidermal junction

- Pictured below: SSSS in a newborn with generalized bullous epidermolysis


Photo credit: K. Kouakou, M. E. Dainguy, K. Kassi, "Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome in Neonate", Case Reports in Dermatological Medicine, vol. 2015, Article ID 901968, 4 pages, 2015. https://doi.org/10.1155/2015/901968; CNX OpenStax, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-0a835f5a88435761042e.text: {{c1::Erythema multiforme}} may appear 1 - 2 weeks after herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection
mss-0a835f5a88435761042e.extra:
- Appears as a target lesion with a pale, pink ring around a dark red ("dusky") center

- Diagnosed clinically - no confirmatory testing needed

- Erythema multiforme minor: localized target lesions without mucosal involvement

- Erythema multiforme major: extensive mucosal compromise that is potentially life-threatening

mss-3f552296eab26573d6ff.text: Black necrotic skin lesions seen in patients with {{c2::Pseudomonas}} bacteremia are indicative of {{c1::ecthyma gangrenosum}}
mss-3f552296eab26573d6ff.extra:
- Ecthyma gangrenosum occurs from perivascular invasion and release of tissue-destructive exotoxins, causing vascular destruction and insufficient blood flow
- Common in neutropenic, hospitalized, or burn patients, or patients with catheters

- Tx: Intravenous antibiotics, NO surgical debridement needed


Photo credit: Abbas et al., CC BY 4.0, via Frontiers in Microbiology; the supplementary image with overlays of the relevant areas was adapted from the image mentioned previously (© AnkiHub, LLC)
